question: What does the Bible say about baptism?
intro: Baptism is the rite with water in which Christ's followers are baptized, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19) or in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 2:38). Among the churches whose readings are set out here, all agree that Christ commanded it, and they read the text differently on who is to be baptized, on what baptism gives or shows, and, on a separate question, on how the water is applied. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that Christ's followers are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as Matthew 28:19 has it (Oneness Pentecostal bodies, noted under the third reading, baptize in the name of Jesus alone, while the Church of God and the Foursquare Church name the threefold name in their statements, and the Assemblies of God statement cites Matthew 28:19); that there is one baptism, as there is one Lord and one faith; and that those baptized are baptized into Christ and into his death, as Romans 6:3 says. The readings differ over who is to be baptized, over what baptism gives or shows, and, on a separate question, over whether the water is poured or the person immersed. A few bodies, such as the Quakers and the Salvation Army, do not practice water baptism; this page does not set out their readings.

passages.quote: make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
one Lord, one faith, one baptism;
all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?
For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

readings.label: Baptism as God's act of cleansing and new birth, given to believers and to the children of believers
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of baptism as the act in which God forgives sin, gives new birth and the Spirit, and joins a person to Christ and his church, so that texts such as Acts 2:38 and Titus 3:5 name what baptism itself does. They baptize infants as well as converts, taking the promise of Acts 2:39 and the household baptisms to include children. Catholic teaching speaks of the sacrament as working by Christ's act and not by the worth of the minister, counts baptism with water in the Trinitarian name in other churches as valid and not to be repeated (Catechism 1271-1272), names triple immersion the most expressive way and accepts pouring (Catechism 1239). Eastern Orthodox practice is threefold immersion (Longer Catechism, questions 288-290), joined with anointing (chrismation) and communion, normally in infancy; the Longer Catechism grounds infant baptism in the faith of parents and sponsors and in baptism's taking the place of circumcision (Colossians 2:11-12). Lutheran teaching holds baptism valid by God's word whether or not the recipient believes, and faith the means by which its gifts are received (Large Catechism, on Baptism). Anglican teaching holds this reading together with the second: the Church of England's Article XXVII calls baptism a sign of regeneration or new birth, and Anglican members hold the reading in varying measure. Wesleyan and Methodist members hold it in part: the Articles of Religion held by the United Methodist Church (Article XVII) call baptism a sign of regeneration or new birth, and its statement By Water and the Spirit calls baptism the means of entry into new life in Christ; the same statement holds that the new birth may not always coincide with the moment of baptism, and that the sacrament is received once, and John Wesley taught that baptism is not itself the new birth (Standard Sermon 45).

passages.quote: Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
passages.note: Read as saying that baptism is for the forgiveness of sins and comes with the Spirit's gift.

passages.quote: Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name.
passages.note: Read as joining baptism with the washing away of sins.

passages.quote: no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit.
passages.note: Read as naming baptism together with the Spirit in new birth; other readers take “water” otherwise.

passages.quote: through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
passages.note: The Greek word the Berean renders “new birth” is glossed “regeneration”; read as baptism's washing.

passages.quote: the baptism that now saves you also
passages.note: Read as saying what baptism does, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
passages.context_note: This is one clause of a longer sentence: 'this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also-not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God-through the resurrection of Jesus Christ' (3:21; the sentence continues into 3:22). The quote here is its first part; readings 2 and 3 quote the middle.

passages.quote: This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off
passages.note: Read as including children in the promise that is spoken with baptism.
passages.context_note: The promise is named in the verse before: 'you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.' The sentence ends 'to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.'

passages.quote: he and all his household were baptized.
passages.note: Read as a baptism that included the children of the house.
passages.context_note: The promise in 16:31 is 'you and your household'. The word of the Lord was spoken 'to him and to everyone in his house' (16:32), and afterwards 'he and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe in God' (16:34).

passages.quote: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved
passages.note: Believing and being baptized joined to being saved. The site marks Mark 16:9-20 as absent from the earliest manuscripts, which end Mark after verse 8; the churches that cite this verse here read the longer ending as Scripture.

passages.quote: having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God
passages.note: Paul says believers were buried with Christ in baptism and raised with him through faith in God's power.

passages.quote: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation
passages.note: Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation; the old has passed away.

passages.quote: buried with Him through baptism into death
passages.note: Paul says believers were buried with Christ through baptism into death so they may walk in newness of life.

passages.quote: when she and her household had been baptized
passages.note: Luke records that Lydia and her household were baptized.

passages.quote: in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body
passages.note: Paul says all believers were baptized in one Spirit into one body, Jews or Greeks, slave or free.

passages.quote: I also baptized the household of Stephanas
passages.note: Paul says he also baptized the household of Stephanas.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take cases such as Acts 10:44-47, where the Spirit falls before baptism, and Luke 23:43, to show that God is free to give what he gives apart from the rite, and take Acts 2:38 and Titus 3:5 to name the ordinary way he gives it. Catholic teaching speaks here of baptism of desire. They take the places where baptism follows hearing and believing (Acts 8:12, Acts 18:8) as accounts of adults newly come to faith, and they take 1 Corinthians 1:17 to concern Paul's task of preaching and not the worth of baptism. Eastern Orthodox members also cite Colossians 2:11-12, where baptism is named with circumcision, for the baptism of infants (Longer Catechism, questions 293-294).

readings.label: Baptism as the sign and seal of God's covenant promise, given to believers and to their children
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take baptism to be the New Testament's sign of the covenant God made with Abraham and his descendants, as circumcision was its sign (Colossians 2:11-12). What baptism shows is washing, union with Christ and the Spirit's work; what it seals is God's promise, which faith receives. They baptize infants as well as converts, taking the promise to “you and your children” (Acts 2:39) and the household baptisms to follow Genesis 17, where the sign was given to the children of the house. Reformed teaching calls baptism a sign and seal, baptizes the infants of one or both believing parents (Westminster Confession 28.4), and holds that the Spirit gives what it signifies as God wills. Anglican teaching holds this reading together with the first: Article XXVII speaks of the promises of forgiveness and adoption as visibly signed and sealed, and the catechism of the Anglican Church in North America calls infant baptism a sign of the covenant promise. United Methodist teaching (By Water and the Spirit) calls the baptism of infants and adults the sign of the covenant, as circumcision was the sign of the older covenant; Wesleyan and Methodist members also baptize adult converts, and some hold the first reading as well. The Westminster Confession names pouring or sprinkling and says dipping of the person is not necessary (28.3), and United Methodist teaching accepts sprinkling, pouring or immersion.

passages.quote: an everlasting covenant between Me and you and your descendants after you, to be your God and the God of your descendants after you.
passages.note: In Genesis the covenant is made with Abraham and his descendants; holders of this reading take baptism to be the sign of that same covenant.

passages.quote: every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old, including those born in your household
passages.note: In Genesis the sign, circumcision, is given to infant males and to those born in the household; holders of this reading take baptism to stand where circumcision stood.

passages.quote: he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.
passages.note: A sign that is also called a seal: the words behind “sign and seal”.

passages.quote: with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands.
passages.note: Circumcision is named in the verse before baptism.

passages.quote: And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead.
passages.note: Read as setting baptism where circumcision stood.

passages.quote: This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off
passages.note: Read as the covenant promise reaching the children, as it reached Abraham's.
passages.context_note: The promise is named in the verse before: 'you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.' The sentence ends 'to all whom the Lord our God will call to Himself.'

passages.quote: They were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.
passages.note: Read as the New Testament naming the crossing of the sea, which included Israel's children, a baptism.

passages.quote: Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.
passages.note: Read as calling the children of a believing parent holy, as belonging to the covenant.
passages.context_note: The case is a believer married to an unbeliever who 'is willing to live with' them (7:12-13). In the same verse the word is also said of the spouse: 'the unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband.'

passages.quote: the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus
passages.note: Paul says Christ redeemed us so the blessing promised to Abraham would reach the Gentiles and we receive the promise of the Spirit by faith.

passages.quote: Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these
passages.note: Jesus is indignant at those who keep children away and says the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

passages.quote: Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins
passages.note: Peter's call to repent and be baptized, in the sentence just before the promise 'to you and your children' in verse 39.

passages.quote: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God
passages.note: Peter says the baptism that now saves is not the removal of dirt from the body but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God, through Christ's resurrection.

passages.quote: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession
passages.note: Peter calls his readers a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the sayings that join baptism with forgiveness and salvation (Acts 2:38, Acts 22:16, 1 Peter 3:21) as the language of signs, in which a sign is named for what it points to, as with the circumcision that Romans 4:11 calls a seal of a righteousness already had by faith. They take the baptisms of Acts 8:12 and Acts 18:8 as accounts of adults who came to faith and were baptized, as Abraham believed before he was circumcised, and take “not the removal of dirt from the body” in 1 Peter 3:21 to place the weight on what the water points to.

readings.label: Baptism of those who believe: obedience to Christ's command and a public answer to the gospel
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament's baptisms to follow hearing the gospel, believing and repenting, so that baptism belongs to those who profess faith in Christ, as in Acts 2:41 and Acts 8:12. They take baptism to picture the believer's union with Christ's death and rising (Romans 6:4), to be the believer's public answer to the gospel, and to be a step into the life of the church. Baptist and free-church readers call it an ordinance, a rite Christ commanded and his followers obey, and speak of grace received before baptism and shown in it. Southern Baptists (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article VII) make baptism a prerequisite to church membership and to the Lord's Supper. Pentecostal churches share this practice: the Church of God and the Foursquare Church name the threefold name in their statements, the Assemblies of God statement cites Matthew 28:19, and Oneness Pentecostal bodies baptize in the name of Jesus alone, on Acts 2:38. Pentecostal churches distinguish baptism in water from what they call baptism in the Spirit, with members differing on what water baptism itself gives; Charismatic members within other traditions follow the practice of those traditions. Anabaptist readers (a name given by their opponents in the sixteenth century, meaning those who baptize again; they hold that the baptism they had received as infants was not baptism) speak of baptism as a pledge to follow Christ within the community, and their members differ on how it relates to grace. The 1995 Mennonite confession calls baptism a sign and speaks of being baptized into Christ and his body by the Spirit, water and blood, the last being the offering of one's life, the commitment to love enemies and renounce violence. On the mode, the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 describes baptism as the immersion of a believer and the 1689 London Confession calls immersion necessary to its due administration; the Assemblies of God and the Church of God name immersion; the Mennonite confession accepts pouring, immersion or sprinkling.

passages.quote: Those who embraced his message were baptized,
passages.note: Baptism follows receiving the message.

passages.quote: when they believed Philip as he preached the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
passages.note: Belief first, then baptism.

passages.quote: Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip baptized him.
passages.note: Going down into the water, read as pointing to immersion.

passages.quote: Can anyone withhold the water to baptize these people? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have!
passages.note: Baptism asked for those who had already received the Spirit.

passages.quote: many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized.
passages.note: Hearing, believing, then baptism.

passages.quote: buried with Him through baptism into death
passages.note: Burial and rising with Christ, read as a picture of immersion and of the believer's new life.

passages.quote: You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.
passages.note: Sonship through faith, named in the verse before “baptized into Christ”.

passages.quote: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God
passages.note: Baptism as a pledge made to God from a clear conscience.
passages.context_note: This is one clause of a longer sentence, and it begins before the quote: 'this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also'. It goes on: 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven' (3:21-22).

passages.quote: As soon as Jesus was baptized, He went up out of the water
passages.note: Matthew records that when Jesus was baptized he went up out of the water, and the Spirit of God descended on him.

passages.quote: having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God
passages.note: Paul says believers were buried with Christ in baptism and raised with him through faith in God's power.

passages.quote: Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ
passages.note: Peter calls his hearers to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; the sentence goes on 'for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'

passages.quote: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved
passages.note: In the longer ending of Mark, which the earliest manuscripts lack: Jesus says whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, and whoever does not believe will be condemned. The site marks Mark 16:9-20 as absent from the earliest manuscripts, which end Mark after verse 8; the churches that cite this verse here read the longer ending as Scripture.

passages.quote: John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there
passages.note: John baptized at Aenon near Salim because water was plentiful there.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Acts 2:38 and Acts 22:16 as describing the response of one who repents and calls on the Lord's name, with baptism as its outward form, and take Mark 16:16 to place condemnation on the one who does not believe and not on the one who is not baptized. They take the household texts to describe households who heard the word and rejoiced in believing (Acts 16:32, Acts 16:34, Acts 18:8), and Colossians 2:11-12 to speak of those “raised with Him through your faith.” They take the covenant of Genesis 17 as fulfilled in a people gathered by faith in Christ, and take Acts 2:39 with the words that follow it in Acts 2:41, where those who embraced the message were baptized. Holders who distinguish baptism in the Spirit from baptism in water take Acts 1:5, “For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit,” as the promise of that baptism, and Acts 19:5, “On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus,” as baptism that follows hearing. They take Mark 10:14 with Mark 10:16, where Jesus takes the children in his arms and blesses them, as a blessing and not a baptism; Acts 16:15 and 1 Corinthians 1:16 as households whose members the text does not name, with 1 Corinthians 16:15 saying of the household of Stephanas that they devoted themselves to the service of the saints; and 1 Corinthians 12:13 as the Spirit placing believers in the one body.

terms.note: The Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist word for a rite in which God acts. Eastern Orthodox churches also speak of a holy mystery.
The Baptist and free-church word for a rite Christ commanded and his followers obey.
The word the 1995 Mennonite confession uses for baptism and the Lord's Supper, where other traditions say sacrament or ordinance.
The Reformed phrase, also found in the Church of England's Article XXVII, for baptism as the visible sign of God's promise and its seal, drawing on Romans 4:11.
The baptism of the infant children of believers, practiced by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches.
The Baptist and free-church phrase for baptism of those who have professed faith, as the Pentecostal and Anabaptist traditions also practice it.

A phrase for the teaching that new birth is given in baptism. Those who hold the substance of it often use their own words, such as new birth, illumination or the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5), and some who reject the phrase hold a related view.

The Catholic phrase (Latin for “by the work done”) for the teaching that the sacrament gives grace by Christ's act and not by the worth of the minister, to one who does not place an obstacle in its way.
The Eastern Orthodox anointing with oil that follows baptism and is the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The Pentecostal and Charismatic phrase for an experience of the Spirit that they distinguish from baptism in water. 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Acts 1:5 are among the verses cited for it, and traditions differ on how it relates to baptism in water.

How the water is applied. Those who hold immersion cite Romans 6:4, Acts 8:38 and John 3:23. Those who hold pouring or sprinkling cite Ezekiel 36:25 and Hebrews 10:22, and the number baptized in one day at Acts 2:41. Baptist confessions treat immersion as required: the 1689 London Confession calls it necessary to the due administration of baptism, while the Westminster Confession says dipping of the person is not necessary. Churches differ on this question too, and each reading's summary gives the modes that the documents it cites state.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 7, Decree on the Sacraments, canons on Baptism
further_reading.says: The canons teach that baptism with true water is necessary for salvation, that baptism given in the Trinitarian name with the intention of doing what the Church does is true baptism even from heretics, that infants are to be baptized and counted among the faithful, and that a validly given baptism is not repeated; the canons on the sacraments in general teach that grace is conferred through the act performed (canon 8) and that a minister in mortal sin still confers the sacrament (canon 12).

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1229-1245 (The Celebration of Baptism)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 1239 calls triple immersion in the baptismal water the most expressive way of performing baptism, and notes that from ancient times baptism could also be given by pouring the water three times over the candidate's head.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1246-1255 (Who Can Receive Baptism; infant baptism, 1250-1252)
further_reading.says: It teaches that the practice of infant baptism is an immemorial tradition of the Church, and that the gratuitousness of the grace of salvation is particularly manifest in infant baptism.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1262-1274 (The Grace of Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism purifies from sin and gives new birth in the Holy Spirit, makes a new creature and an adopted child of God, and incorporates into the Church; paragraph 1271 calls it the sacramental bond of unity among all who are reborn through it, and 1272 teaches that it seals the Christian with an indelible mark and cannot be repeated.

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decree 16
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is of the highest necessity for salvation, that infants need it because of original sin, and that it remits original sin and blots out all sin committed before baptism.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 288-294
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is a sacrament in which a believer is thrice plunged in water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, that threefold immersion is the essential act, that children are baptized on the faith of their parents and sponsors, and that baptism takes the place of circumcision, citing Colossians 2:11-12 (questions 293-294).

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article IX (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is necessary to salvation, that through it God's grace is offered, that children are to be baptized, and it condemns the Anabaptists who reject infant baptism.

further_reading.title: Luther's Small Catechism, Part IV (The Sacrament of Holy Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is water comprehended in God's command and connected with God's word, and that it works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to those who believe the promise.

further_reading.title: Luther's Large Catechism, Part Fourth (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism is valid even where faith is wanting, because it rests on God's word and command and faith receives it, and that infants are baptized in the hope that they believe; it describes the act as being sunk under the water and drawn out again.

further_reading.title: Martin Luther, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, 1520, the section on the sacrament of baptism
further_reading.says: Luther describes baptism as a divine promise received by faith and not earned by works, in which forgiveness and new life are given, and as a lifelong reality of dying and rising that the believer returns to.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 28 (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: Chapter 28 calls baptism a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, says dipping of the person is not necessary and pouring or sprinkling is right, says the infants of one or both believing parents are to be baptized, and says grace is not inseparably tied to the water and its efficacy is not tied to the moment it is administered.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 94 and 95
further_reading.says: Question 94 teaches that baptism is washing with water in the threefold name that signifies and seals union with Christ, and question 95 teaches that the infants of members of the visible church are to be baptized.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 165 and 166
further_reading.says: Question 165 teaches that baptism is a sacrament and a sign and seal of union with Christ and of regeneration, and question 166 teaches that infants descending from parents, either both or one of them, professing faith in Christ are within the covenant and are to be baptized.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 69-74
further_reading.says: Question 72 teaches that only Jesus Christ's blood and the Holy Spirit cleanse from sin, question 73 that baptism assures us we are as truly washed of our sins as our bodies are washed with water, and question 74 that infants as well as adults are included in God's covenant and receive baptism in the place of circumcision, citing Colossians 2:11-13.

further_reading.title: Belgic Confession, Article 34 (The Holy Sacrament of Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that Christ ended circumcision and established baptism in its place, that baptism does for believers' children what circumcision did for the Jewish people, and that the children of believers are to be baptized and sealed with the sign of the covenant.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 4, chapter 15 (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: Calvin describes baptism as the sign by which believers are admitted into the church and ingrafted into Christ, a sealed assurance of forgiveness, in which the water itself does not cleanse.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 4, chapter 16 (Paedobaptism)
further_reading.says: Calvin argues that baptism takes the place of circumcision and signifies the same promise under the same covenant, so that the children of believers receive the sign as Jewish infants received circumcision.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Article XXVII (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: Article XXVII calls baptism a sign of regeneration or new birth, says the promises of forgiveness and adoption are visibly signed and sealed by it, and says the baptism of young children is to be retained in the Church.

further_reading.title: To Be a Christian: An Anglican Catechism (2019), question 129
further_reading.says: The catechism calls infant baptism a sign of God's promise that infants are embraced in the covenant community.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Articles XVI and XVII
further_reading.says: Article XVI names baptism and the Lord's Supper as the two sacraments ordained by Christ, and Article XVII calls baptism a sign of regeneration or the new birth and says the baptism of young children is to be retained.

further_reading.title: By Water and the Spirit: A United Methodist Understanding of Baptism (1996)
further_reading.says: This official statement calls baptism the means of entry into new life in Christ and the sign of the covenant for infants and adults, as circumcision was for the older covenant, says the new birth may not always coincide with the moment of baptism, says the sacrament is received only once, and allows sprinkling, pouring or immersion.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 45 (The New Birth), section IV
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that baptism is not the new birth, that baptism is the outward sign and the new birth the inward change, and that the Church of England supposes those baptized in infancy to be born again at the same time.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article VII (Baptism and the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: It describes baptism as the immersion of a believer in water, and makes it a church ordinance and a prerequisite to the privileges of church membership and to the Lord's Supper.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 29 (Of Baptism)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 2 names those who profess repentance towards God and faith in Christ as the proper subjects of baptism, and paragraph 4 calls immersion necessary to its due administration.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths, 6 (The Ordinances of the Church), a. Baptism in Water
further_reading.says: The statement commands baptism by immersion for all who repent and believe, as a declaration to the world of dying with Christ and rising to walk in newness of life, and cites Matthew 28:19; it does not itself state the baptismal formula.

further_reading.title: Church of God Declaration of Faith
further_reading.says: It teaches water baptism by immersion, for all who repent, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

further_reading.title: Foursquare Declaration of Faith, article IX (Water Baptism and the Lord's Supper)
further_reading.says: The Declaration calls water baptism in the threefold name a blessed outward sign of an inward work.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 11 (Baptism), commentary
further_reading.says: It teaches the baptism of believers as a sign of repentance and cleansing and a pledge to serve Christ, names baptism by the Spirit, water and blood, says infants are safe in God's care and need no baptism, and says the church may baptize by pouring, immersion or sprinkling.

further_reading.title: Schleitheim Confession (1527), Article I (Baptism)
further_reading.says: Article I gives baptism to those who have learned repentance and amendment of life and believe that Christ has taken away their sins, and rejects infant baptism.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1257-1261 (The Necessity of Baptism)
further_reading.says: It teaches that God has bound salvation to the sacrament of baptism but is not himself bound by his sacraments (1257), that those who die for the faith before baptism are counted as baptized through their death (1258), and that catechumens who die before baptism are assured of salvation by their explicit desire for it, their repentance and their charity (1259).

further_reading.title: The Orthodox Faith, Volume II (Worship): The Sacraments, Chrismation (Orthodox Church in America)
further_reading.says: It says that chrismation is always done in the Orthodox Church together with baptism, and that baptism and chrismation are fulfilled in the newly baptized receiving Holy Communion at the liturgy straight away, as with infants so with adults.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked: Matt 28:19 (clause), Eph 4:5, Rom 6:3 (clause), Gal 3:26, 3:27; Acts 2:38, 2:39 (clause, the verse's hyphen not reached), 2:41 (clause), 8:12 (clause from 'when'), 8:38, 10:47 (the verse's curly quotes dropped), 16:15 (clause), 16:33 (clause), 18:8 (clause), 22:16 (clause, the trailing quotation mark of the server text dropped); Titus 3:5 (clause); John 3:5 (clause); Mark 16:16 (clause); 1 Pet 3:21 (two clauses, in R1 and R3); Rom 4:11 (clause), 6:4 (clause); Col 2:11 (clause), 2:12; Gen 17:7 (clause), 17:12 (clause); 1 Cor 7:14. Verses named in answers or terms but not quoted were read too: Luke 23:43, Acts 10:44, Acts 16:32, 16:34, 1 Cor 1:17, 12:13, Ezek 36:25, Heb 10:22, John 3:23, Acts 1:5 (reads 'you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit', so it exists with the wording the Pentecostal term names). ORDER: R1 first because it states the practice and sense of the early church's life as its holders read it (Catholic and Orthodox formal statements are later, Trent 1547 and the councils); R2 and R3 were both set out in the 1520s (Zurich), so the order between them is a judgment, not a ranking, and a reviewer may swap them; the order does not rank. THREE READINGS: the usual split is infants versus believers, which hides the second axis (what baptism gives). The three readings cross both axes: R1 infants and believers, baptism as God's cleansing act; R2 infants and believers, baptism as covenant sign; R3 believers only, baptism as a public sign of grace received. Nobody is folded into an opponent's reading. R1 and R2 are not collapsed because Reformed and Lutheran readers both baptize infants and differ sharply on what baptism gives. PASSAGES: 14, 13 and 13 after the 2026-10-26 verse audit (eight each before it). Mark 16:16 is in R1 (and answered in R3); it is marked on the site as absent from the earliest manuscripts, and the note says so. Acts 8:37 is absent from the Berean text and is not quoted. MODE: handled as a smaller point, in the summaries (each notes the mode its holders use), in the mode term, and with Rom 6:4, Acts 8:38 in R3's passages; Ezek 36:25 and Heb 10:22 are named in the term only (John 3:23 is now a passage of R3). HELD_BY: assignments are approximate and each summary says where a tradition holds a reading in part or its members differ (Anglican in R1 and R2; Wesleyan / Methodist in R2; Pentecostal / Charismatic and Anabaptist in R3). Lutheran appears only in R1 though some Lutheran statements stress faith in the infant, which I did not claim. Nothing names a person, scholar or leader. TRADITIONS NOT ON THE LIST: Quaker and Salvation Army practice (no water baptism) is outside the list and the agreed block says 'Christ's followers are baptized', which they do not describe in the same way; a reviewer should say whether the agreed summary needs 'in the churches below' added. WORDS: the summaries, answers and notes were checked for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely'; 'but' appears only inside quoted verses (1 Cor 7:14, 1 Pet 3:21). A reviewer may reword 'and not' phrases, which state a tradition's own contrast. LEFT OUT: (a) the question of baptism of the dying, of unbaptized infants and of the thief on the cross, apart from the one mention of Luke 23:43; (b) rebaptism and who may baptize; (c) the formula (the name of Jesus alone, as in Acts 2:38, against the threefold name in Matt 28:19), which some Oneness Pentecostal bodies hold and which is a separate question from this card; (d) Luke 18:15, the blessing of children, which holders of infant baptism cite (Mark 10:14 is now a passage of R2); (e) the baptisms of John (Mark 1:4, Acts 19:4) and of Jesus (Matt 3:16), and the Old Testament washings, which an OT reviewer or a rabbi may want to say more about: Ezek 36:25 and the washings of the law are touched only in the mode term. RELATED IDS: card ids baptism, circumcision, repentance, forgiveness, covenant, faith, salvation, household were each fetched from /api/entity and found; grace was listed as present (missing false) in the faith hub's leads but not fetched on its own. Theme ids deliverance, church, spirit, covenant, children_of_god, mercy_restoration are all listed by /api/majorthemes. UNRESOLVED: (1) Acts 16:34 as the Berean words it says the jailer 'and all his household rejoiced that they had come to believe'; the Greek participle for believing is singular (the jailer 'having believed', rejoicing with his whole household), which R1 and R2 holders cite and R3 answers cite differently; the card follows the Berean for R3's answer and a reviewer may want a line on the Greek. (2) Whether 'Eastern Orthodox' should hold the 'Orthodox practice is full immersion' sentence in R1's summary, which I wrote from general knowledge; confirm.
